articles.title: How do horror novelists celebrate Halloween? ‘Whimsical witch stuff’ and vintage radio shows
articles.summary: Four horror novelists – Riley Sager, Leah Rowan, Rachel Harrison and Grady Hendrix – share advice for embracing Halloween, even if you’re a scaredy cat. What do the best Halloween costumes all have in common?
body: In October, horror lovers can finally rejoice in the season’s endless supply of spooky films, haunted houses and macabre decor.
Others prefer to bask in the comforting glow of the TV while enjoying their 70th rewatch of Hocus Pocus (which arguably is scarier than you might think).

No matter what camp you fall into, you can still enjoy October, or “spooky season” as millennials call it. So I asked the most qualified people I could think of – horror novelists – how to enjoy the season.

“We don’t need to love Freddy and Jason to love horror. It’s a very broad spectrum,” said Rachel Harrison, bestselling author of the witchy novel Cackle and the haunting read, Play Nice. Riley Sager, author of The Unknown and Home Before Dark, suggests a low-key alternative: spooky vintage radio shows. “They are not terrifying. They’re just chilling,” he said. (His recommendations include Three Keleton Key and Sorry Wrong Number.) They also shared how they celebrate the season and, perhaps most importantly, their favorite Halloween candy.
points: Four horror novelists – Riley Sager, Leah Rowan, Rachel Harrison and Grady Hendrix – share advice for embracing Halloween, even if you’re a scaredy cat.

articles.title: The kindness of strangers: After a tearful breakup dinner, another patron paid our bill
articles.summary: When I was in an emotionally vulnerable state, that unexpected gesture took the edge off a very sad evening. The breakup came out of the blue. My then girlfriend and I had shared an intense and fast-moving relationship for two years, then one day she ended things over the phone.
body: I was quite upset to have been dumped over the phone, and managed to get her to agree to meet me for dinner a couple of weeks later. At a restaurant, we shared a very tearful and intimate conversation about what we meant to each other. She didn’t reconsider her decision, though – that was it.

When it came time to get the cheque, we were told the bill had already been paid by another patron who wished to remain anonymous. Someone within earshot of us must have heard our conversation and decided to extend a kindness.

It was completely unexpected – we’re not raised to expect such generosity in western society. When I was in an emotionally vulnerable state, that act calmed me, and took the edge off all we had discussed at dinner.

My former girlfriend and I went our separate ways that evening but have kept in sporadic contact over the years. We still agree that we had a positive influence on each other’s lives. And we will always remember how a stranger gave us a very sweet ending to a very sad evening.

articles.title: Dua Lipa Knows a Good Book—and a Great Look
articles.summary: At London’s Literature Festival, guest curator Dua Lipa made a compelling case for literary chic by way of Chanel and Prada alongside Mustafa and Zadie Smith.
body: Dua Lipa’s taste in books is rivaled only by her penchants for some very fabulous fashions. The singer has long made her literary tastes known through her successful Service95 Book Club, but this weekend, she took her love of the written word to the stage, curating a series of conversations for London’s Literature Festival at the Southbank Centre. Her wardrobe was just as carefully considered as her reading list.

On Saturday, Lipa played host to two literary heavyweights at the Royal Festival Hall: acclaimed novelist Zadie Smith, with whom she discussed White Teeth, Smith’s landmark 2000 debut, and Sudanese Canadian poet and musician Mustafa, whose 2025 poetry collection Nour explores love, grief, faith, and devotion. Two very different and expansive conversations, which required two different outfits.

articles.title: Your boss might be an idiot - and 12 other things you need to know about work | Emma Beddington
articles.summary: British teenagers are stressing about jobs (or the lack of them). Here is my advice, from owning your mistakes to the importance of biscuits. Young people want to know more about the world of work.
body: It’s sensible stuff – dispiritingly so. Shouldn’t they be drinking BuzzBallz at bus stops? If someone had asked 13-year-old me what I wanted to know about work, I would have stared blankly, or asked: “What job will let me touch Mark Shaw (of obscure 80s band Then Jerico)?” Look at what their French peers are up to!

Anyone who tells you “do something you love and you’ll never work a day in your life” is a cliche-sodden bullshitter. “Do something you love and see your relationship to that thing shift, become ambivalent, maybe even curdle” is more accurate. Most people don’t keep a pure, unsullied passion for the thing they spend 40-plus hours a week doing. “All jobs get boring, even if you’re Mick Jagger,” as a friend says.

You don’t need to know what you want to do yet. Try things out: even jobs you hate are illuminating, and it’s almost always better to do something than nothing. Working somewhere poisonously unethical is the exception.
Your colleagues make more difference – good or bad – to the quality of your life than the work itself. You can’t do much about it, but cherish the nice ones.

articles.title: With governments asking us to stockpile, can we learn anything from disaster films?
articles.summary: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts. Last week’s replies: will there ever again be a band as big as the Beatles or the Stones?
body: A s I was building pyramids of loo roll and tinned beans in response to the government’s Be Ready campaign, launched this week, I got to thinking about what other aspects of modern life might help us to get through an emergency. Specifically, our extensive back catalogue of disaster movies, TV series and the like. We’ve imagined catastrophes hitting the human race in so many ways, with so many different outcomes. Are there any useful tips we can take from our library of entertaining, effects-laden disaster films?

articles.title: From Elizabeth Taylor to Kim Kardashian and Kris Jenner: The Starry History of the Scorpio Cape
articles.summary: At the “All’s Fair” premiere in Rome, Kris Jenner paid homage to Elizabeth Taylor, Grace Kelly, and Kim Kardashian with a piece of fashion history.
body: Kim Kardashian and Kris Jenner have a shared affinity for archival fashion and high-octane glamour, with an increasing penchant for mother-daughter twinning. But their latest red carpet outing came with a particularly storied piece of Hollywood history, involving Elizabeth Taylor, Grace Kelly, and a certain astrological sign of the moment.

At the Rome Film Festival last night, where Kardashian was celebrating the season two premiere of Ryan Murphy’s legal drama All’s Fair, Jenner arrived in a sweeping black velvet hooded cape, its ivory silk lining framing her face and glittering scorpions embroidered across the chest. She wore it with long white gloves and a floor-length white gown underneath.
The striking design was a homage to a Tiziani Roma creation worn by Elizabeth Taylor in 1969, when the actor attended Princess Grace of Monaco’s 40th birthday celebrations.

articles.title: Where to Stay When Visiting Alaska's Denali National Park
articles.summary: The best hotels, lodges, and cabins for a trip to the Last Frontier.
body: With broad river valleys, colorful meadows peppered with fireweed and lupine, forests thick with spruce and aspen, and the snow-covered Alaska Range rising in the distance, Denali National Park and Preserve is one of those places that can still feel startlingly wild no matter how many times you visit. At 6.1 million acres, it’s larger than Massachusetts, and the sheer scale of the national park means a trip here can look very different depending on where you choose to stay.

I’ve selected the best stays across that spectrum, from full-service hotels and family-friendly cabins to secluded backcountry lodges and even a chalet set on a glacier just miles from the summit of North America’s highest peak. Read on for my favorite places to stay near Denali National Park in Alaska.

articles.title: From the Archives: America’s Enduring Appetite for Candy
articles.summary: With Halloween treats on his mind, Jeffrey Steingarten investigates America's enduring appetite for candy.
body: “Dream Sweets,” by Jeffrey Steingarten, was originally published in the October 2009 issue of Vogue.

Whether you're four or 40, it's never too early to start planning for Halloween. And planning means candy. If you're an average American, you consume a half-pound of candy a week, a good deal more around Halloween. If you're a way subaverage American, you may be in trouble. Remember the study about ten years ago from the Harvard School of Public Health? People who eat candy live longer than people who eat none at all. Eat candy or die? No, the figures are not quite so dramatic as that. But don't say I didn't warn you.

Papabubble, on Broome Street in Little Italy, arrived from Barcelona shortly before Halloween 2007. They sell only hard candy, made fresh daily, by hand, right before your eyes, each piece a gaily striped little cylinder that reminds you of Christmas. The flavors change—tomorrow, they say, they'll add watermelon and passion fruit. The tiny, beautiful shop is shiny with white tile, stainless steel, and pale wood, and one wall is stacked with candy whose intricate designs and rainbow flavors produce an infinite variety.
points: With Halloween treats on his mind, Jeffrey Steingarten investigates America's enduring appetite for candy.

articles.title: Drake Celebrates 40 With a Big Rolex, Free Birkins, and the Backstreet Boys
articles.summary: The rapper rang in a new decade with a sparkling tuxedo and a birthday weekend that spared no expense.
body: You only turn 40 once, and Drake made sure to usher in his fifth decade with a birthday extravaganza to remember. There were surprise performance by the Backstreet Boys, Hermès and Chanel handbags handed out as party favors, and cash prizes reaching an eye-watering $1 million. Drizzy’s outfits were just as extravagant across his entire birthday weekend.

On Friday night, Drake welcomed more than 400 guests to New York’s Casa Cipriani for the first of two birthday celebrations, swapping his recent bohemian proclivities for something more dapper. Just a day earlier, he’d been spotted enjoying a pre-birthday dinner at Mamo in Manhattan, wrapped in a chestnut-brown fringed shawl that wouldn’t have looked out of place in Sienna Miller’s fall wardrobe. But for the main event, the rapper was firmly in black-tie mode, opting for a sparkling black tuxedo jacket with silk lapels, pleated and wide-legged suit trousers, a crisp white shirt, and a satin bow tie adored with a diamond “D” pin.
points: The rapper rang in a new decade with a sparkling tuxedo and a birthday weekend that spared no expense.
